Is your marketing automation platform helping you grow, or making it harder to adapt? Jon Miller, co-founder of Marketo, Engagio, and Phave, joined me on the SEJ Podcast to discuss where he believes legacy marketing systems fall short and how AI could change the way B2B teams work.

In our conversation, Miller explained why individual leads and company accounts can miss the complexity of buying groups, how campaign queues and extra tools can signal gaps in your platform, and the difference between AI that builds rules-based workflows and AI that makes decisions. He also shares why marketers should review renewal dates early and think carefully before committing to a multi-year contract.

[00:40] Meet Jon Miller [01:26] Why Miller Built Phave [04:25] Rethinking The B2B Marketing Playbook [06:11] Moving From Rules To AI Reasoning [07:58] Why Buying Groups Matter [09:40] Signs Your Marketing Stack Is Holding You Back [12:47] AI That Builds Automation Versus AI That Is The Automation [15:20] Reviewing Your Platform Before Renewal [17:09] Where To Find Jon Miller

Editor’s Note: This transcript has been edited for clarity and readability.

Heather Campbell: Thanks so much for joining us for today’s SEJ Podcast. I am your host, Heather Campbell, and I’ve got a guest who helped build the tools most of us have been running our marketing on for the last 20 years.

With me is Jon Miller. He is one of the people who invented the modern B2B marketing stack, and now he’s trying to replace it. I thought having him on our podcast would help marketing leaders take a look at whether the platforms you’re running could be causing gaps in the insights and data you need to grow your business.

Jon co-founded Marketo and was its CMO. He helped take it to a billion-dollar IPO, and the company went on to a $4.7 billion sale to Adobe. Then he did it again: He founded Engagio in 2015, an account-based marketing platform acquired by Demandbase in 2020, and ran their marketing through 2023.

Jon knows a thing or two about growth, and growth is where so many marketers and business leaders are stuck right now. That’s why I wanted to have you on the show. Jon, welcome.

Heather: As I learned about you and Phave.com, the newest platform you’ve just released, it’s barely even three weeks ago, right?

Heather: Tell us about what you saw breaking in traditional martech tools that made you want to compete with your own creation, thinking about Marketo. What gaps in current martech meant we marketers needed something new? What were you seeing?

Jon: First off, I love the name Phave for the company because it has such a positive association and it’s very short. The problem is I have to tell you how to spell it, which I think a search-focused audience might appreciate. It’s Phave with a PH: P-H-A-V-E.

With every other company, I’ve focused on wanting you to know how to spell it. Marketo and Engagio were pretty clear. I considered calling this company Conducto to put it into the same family, but ultimately decided Phave was better.

We launched Phave just over two and a half weeks ago after being in stealth for a while. For those who don’t know, Phave is AI-native marketing automation. It’s meant to replace legacy marketing automation platforms like Marketo, HubSpot, Eloqua, and Pardot.

As you alluded to, over 20 years ago, I was the founder of one of those platforms, Marketo. I’m proud of what we built. So many people come up to me who have literally built their careers on Marketo. That gives me such a positive feeling.

At the same time, when I decided to start a new company and was talking to people during my research, so many expressed frustration with the legacy platforms, using words like “necessary evil” to describe them.

I realized there was a lot of latent frustration with the lack of innovation in the category, especially since Marketo went to Adobe, Eloqua went to Oracle, and Pardot went to Salesforce.

People weren’t really moving on. There wasn’t much platform switching because there wasn’t anything worth switching to, and nobody likes a migration. So I set out to build it.

Jon: I didn’t want to build something a little better. Nobody is going to migrate for something a little better. There were two key principles behind Phave.

First, I wanted to build something for what I call the new B2B playbook. We built Marketo and the other systems for a fairly simplistic model of marketing: Maybe you have an ebook, get people to fill out a form, capture their information, nurture and score them, and pass them to sales at the right time.

It was very focused on new business acquisition and meant to be measurable within this simple, linear machine. That doesn’t reflect how buying works today. I’m not sure it ever really reflected how buying worked.

We know there are complex buying committees. Buying isn’t happening through one person.

Jon: We know a lot of that buying committee is doing research anonymously across channels that are hidden or dark to us. We know the initial land is usually just a small fraction of the total deal value, and we need to do post-sale marketing to retain and expand the relationship.

In many ways, tools like Marketo weren’t built for any of that. When I talk about the new playbook, I mean something that works the way marketing needs to work today.

Jon: That leads to the second principle: AI. AI has dramatically changed both how buyers buy and how we can market to them, and what’s possible.

With Phave, we set out not just to add AI to a marketing automation platform, but to reimagine what a marketing automation platform should be when you have access to modern reasoning AI models.

This lets us move from a world of if-then rules to AI that can think and reason. Rules have a place. They’re good at things that must be true, like “Don’t email someone in Germany if you don’t have double opt-in consent.”

Jon: Rules are bad at handling ambiguity and judgment. The reality is that B2B buying is full of ambiguity and judgment.

Think of all the things we do in a marketing platform: What should this person’s score be? Are they sales-ready? What segment should they belong in? Which rep should I route them to? All the way down to: What actions should I take with this person to move her and her buying group toward an objective I’m trying to achieve?

That requires handling ambiguity, judgment, and reasoning, which rules cannot do. That’s the big unlock. Phave in five minutes: new playbook, AI reasoning, not rules.

Heather: One thing I was drawn to was your statement that leads are too narrow and companies, or accounts, are too broad.

With all the personalization we can do, and knowing that personalization helps move people down the funnel, I like looking at them as buying groups. You have different levels and roles within an organization. That helps you take personalized messaging and give it to the person in that role, wherever they are in the pipeline and their stage right now.

Jon: There are a couple of aspects to where buying groups really matter. You’re referring to understanding each person’s role and persona in the buying group, which is absolutely important.

The other thing is recognizing which product or solution that buying group is about, because that also determines what they’ll find relevant. But the most important thing is: Where is that buying group in its unique journey with you?

The problem with traditional ABM, for example, is that an account buys a product from you, so you call that account a customer. If you market to everybody in the account as though they’re a customer, you’ll be doing the wrong thing for people in buying groups that are buying other products or are at a different stage of the journey.

That’s why buying groups are the right object for B2B, and why leads are too narrow, and accounts are too broad.

Heather: Organizations depend on the data their marketing technology gives them: the insights and dashboards they’ve leaned on for so many years.

For businesses still running on a legacy stack and relying on those, what gaps could it be creating that they’re not aware of? What should they look out for, and why might they want to switch to a different platform and get out of that legacy mindset?

Jon: I’ve seen marketers suffer from what I call “marketing automation Stockholm syndrome.” They’ve had to learn to live with the quirks and idiosyncrasies of these platforms. They take it for granted that this is how things are. When exposed to another way of doing things, their first reaction is, “But that’s not the way things are.”

Your question is: What should prompt you to pick your head up and say there should be something different here, even without talking about the massive transformations AI enables?

I talk to CMOs who are frustrated with how long it takes to go from idea to campaign. They have an idea, and demand gen creates a brief, which they can now do really fast with Claude. But then they hand it to somebody in marketing operations, who puts it into a ticket queue, prioritizes it, and eventually builds the campaign in Marketo two weeks later.

Then it goes back to the demand gen person, and you lose another two weeks on back-and-forth. That isn’t how things need to be, especially in the age of AI. It’s how we’ve learned to live with Marketo’s idiosyncrasies.

Another example is finding yourself buying more and more stuff and expanding your tech stack to fix gaps in your core platform: lead routing, matching leads to accounts, deduplication, and even more sophisticated things like buying groups, post-sale marketing, and bringing in social buying signals.

When you have a legacy platform, these are all things you solve by buying more stuff. Perhaps that’s not the right answer. When you’re looking at your bloated tech stack, ask: Shouldn’t there be a better, simpler way to do this? That’s another signal I’d look at.

Heather: Absolutely. “We’ve always done it that way” is built into too many workflows.

Heather: You’ve drawn a distinction between AI that builds your automation and AI that is the automation. Why should a business leader care which one they’re buying?

Jon: When you have AI that builds the automation, it’s still building a rules-based, if-this-then-that workflow. If you want to account for more factors, scenarios, and nuance, that means more conditions and branches. We’ve all seen how any attempt to do this well quickly ends up with spaghetti: complexity that’s brittle and hard to manage.

Having AI build it for you is a quick recipe for building something more complex, brittle, complicated, and harder to understand, rather than better and smoother. When AI builds it, you’re just paving the cow path in some ways, making the old way faster.

AI that is the automation is when you rethink it so you can do things you couldn’t do before.

As an analogy, before Claude Opus 4.8 came around, engineers were being asked to code. We talked about copilots, where the engineer was still coding, but AI was alongside, making suggestions: “You could do this faster.” Maybe they’d ask it to quickly clean up a subroutine. A year and a half ago, that was state of the art, and it was pretty cool.

Now, the best engineers don’t write code anymore. They go to Cursor, their harness, and say, “This is what I want,” and AI builds it for them. That’s different. AI is the coding, as opposed to helping with the coding.

In some ways, that’s what revolutionized engineering, and I think, if we let it, it will revolutionize marketing.

Heather: As we talk about AI coming in and some of the pivots marketers need to make, we need to look at what we’re tracking, how we’re tracking it, how we’re moving leads down the pipeline, and how we’re thinking about them.

What’s one thing listeners can take back to their desks and implement tomorrow? If they have a legacy system and feel they have gaps, where should they start looking or auditing to decide whether a different platform is right for them?

Jon: The first thing I’d advise anybody on a legacy platform, and this is self-serving, but I also think it’s good advice, is: Do not renew anything for more than a year. The world is moving too fast to lock yourself into a multi-year contract.

Imagine having an old flip phone and locking yourself into a two- or three-year contract a month before the iPhone came out. You’d feel pretty sad when everyone else was doing all this cool stuff, and you were still pressing buttons to send simple text messages.

The first thing I’d do is know when your renewal is up and try to get ahead of it. Depending on the size of your organization, it might take two months or six months to properly evaluate and implement another solution.

Get ahead of that. You may choose Phave or something besides Phave, but don’t let yourself get caught behind a contract and a renewal date. That’s where I’d start.

Heather: That’s great advice. Anytime you’re signing multi-year contracts, it’s good for pricing, but you don’t know what else is coming out that you might miss.

Jon, thank you for your time. I appreciate your insights and everything you’ve shared with our audience. Before I let you go, where can they find you?

Jon: It’s been a pleasure. Thank you for having me on and for the conversation. Professionally, we’re at Phave.com. You can check out a demo, read resources, or contact sales if appropriate.

I’m also on LinkedIn as Jon Miller, writing about all this and more. Come connect and follow me there.

Heather: I appreciate it, Jon. Thank you.

#7448. AI is becoming an information gateway. Audiences still don’t want it making their news.

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

An average of 24% of respondents across nine countries said they’d seen a label noting that content was made with AI in the last week, and 20% had seen a bullet-point AI news summary.

In my Nieman Lab prediction this time last year, I wrote that “in 2026, the use of AI as an information gateway will only rise further.”

As it turns out, I was right. In new research that I published with my colleagues Rasmus Kleis Nielsen and Richard Fletcher, one of our many findings is that generative AI systems are becoming ever more significant information intermediaries, both when intentionally used and when incidentally encountered.

For our new report, “Generative AI and News Report 2026: From Standalone Tools to Information Infrastructure,”  we surveyed audiences across nine countries, including the United States, on their use of AI in their everyday lives, what they think its impact will be on different sectors of society, and what they think about its use in news and journalism specifically. I obviously think you should read the whole report, but here are some of the major takeaways.

The use of standalone conversational AI systems such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini continues to grow rapidly, with 51% of respondents across the six countries where we have past data saying they now use AI weekly (49% in the U.S.). That’s a faster spread, at least in the U.S., than smartphones or the internet saw.

Many people also encounter AI through “incidental” AI exposure in the AI-infused services and platforms they’re already using. Search engines such as Google and Bing are key drivers: 57% of respondents across countries said they saw or engaged with AI-generated answers or summaries in the last week. News media, too, drives AI exposure. An average of 24% of respondents across nine countries said they’d seen a label noting that content was made with AI in the last week, and 20% had seen a bullet-point AI news summary.

Despite all the talk about AI agents, we find that, so far, they haven’t broken into the mainstream. The vast majority of respondents across all nine countries (67%) said they had not used an AI agent in the last week. Fourteen percent used one for a real task and 13% tried one just to experiment.

Our data provides solid evidence that a broader transformation of the information environment is afoot. Conversational AI systems have arrived as information intermediaries. Trust is not the main reason people use them. Instead, people see conversational AI systems as friction-reducing machines that get them information more quickly.

“Getting information” continues to be the most common use case. Thirty-eight percent of respondents across countries (35% in the U.S.) said they had used generative AI for getting information in the last week, up from 24% in 2025 and 11% in 2024.

We looked more closely at what people do when they say they use AI for getting information. Across the six countries we’ve surveyed since 2024, we primarily see a mixture of search-equivalent behaviors like “researching a topic” (24%) or “answering factual questions” (18%). People are also increasingly turning to AI for advice (20%).

Using AI directly for news, meanwhile, remains a niche activity, as we demonstrated in the Digital News Report earlier this year. But that use is increasing: 9% of respondents across our six core countries say they use AI for news, up from 6% in 2025 and 3% in 2024.

Many people don’t hold clear or strong views about whether AI output is trustworthy. But people who do rely on it for information trust it. Across the nine countries, 75% of those who used AI to answer factual questions trusted the answers, as did 76% of those who used it for advice and 72% of those who used it for news. Only small minorities expressed distrust.

At the same time, trust and trustworthiness do not, at this stage, seem to be central to why people rely on AI systems. Instead, people tend to see these systems as friction-reducing machines. The convenience of getting a faster and easier answer was chosen by 64% as the main reason they use AI, followed by the interactivity afforded by natural language interfaces (56%). Only a minority (21%) said they use AI because they get more reliable information from it than from other sources.

As AI systems become widely used, their growing popularity is likely to affect the use of legacy content offerings and digital platforms and services. As my coauthor Rasmus Kleis Nielsen put it on LinkedIn, rapid growth in AI use isn’t just eating into what news sites have to offer. It’s eating into search, too — with people who use AI for information saying they use not just news, but search engines less, too, and by a wider margin. Challenging times may be ahead not just for news publishers, but also for the incumbent digital giants previously seen as unassailable.

As in previous years, we wanted to know what people think of AI’s use in journalism and news. We find that people’s attitudes here are remarkably entrenched and negative — though they also haven’t worsened significantly.

People across countries remain uncomfortable with the use of AI in the newsroom, especially with the idea of news being made entirely or primarily with AI. On average across nine countries, just 12% of respondents say they are very or somewhat comfortable with news made entirely by AI. That figure rises to 19% if there is some human oversight. This has hardly changed since 2024, and the gap between human- and AI-made news appears in every country we surveyed.

This also remains true regardless of whether it is breaking news or reporting. People are even more uncomfortable with AI being used for commentary or opinion — formats where the expectation that a human should share their view is strongest.

Our findings raise several important questions for journalists and publishers navigating the rise of generative AI.

First, generative AI is becoming an increasingly significant information intermediaries, with a number of possible knock-on effects on news. People are using AI to reduce friction by getting “good enough” outputs for some information needs — and skipping legacy platforms, established publishers, and the time and effort it takes to find the best available information. Discovery, brand attribution, data collection, and monetization all grow more challenging for publishers in this context.

Second, even though use continues to grow, the public remains skeptical of AI in news. This isn’t just a challenge for newsrooms’ internal adoption. It also shows that publishers using AI need to communicate to audiences what’s in it for them.

Third, beyond news, our findings speak to wider debates about AI’s societal impact. As in other studies on this topic, we find that uptake of AI is uneven. Weekly use is more common among people in professional occupations than those in entry-level or service occupations. Most people rely on free — usually less advanced — AI models.

The differences in how — not just whether — people use AI may become a new dividing line. As AI researcher and OpenAI cofounder Andrej Karpathy recently argued, there is a widening “gap in shared understanding of LLM capability,” with most people not seeing what has left those inside AI firms both excited and worried.

Expectations of what AI will do differ far more between daily users and people who have never used it than between any other groups in our survey. When two groups form very different views of the same technology because they have such different starting points, there will likely be consequences.

This doesn’t matter just for people’s individual choices around whether and how to make use of AI in their own lives. It also matters where AI is adopted and governed through collective decisions — in public services, for example — that apply to those who do not use it.

Felix Simon is the research fellow in AI, information, and news at the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism and a research associate at the Oxford Internet Institute (OII) at the University of Oxford.

Webinar: 9 AI Workflows For Better Content. Nov 18, 2 PM ET.

Build programmatic SEO pages that earn their place with unique data, launch checks, and pruning rules that keep scaled publishing from becoming spam.

Generative AI has removed the barrier to publishing at scale. A brand can produce thousands of pages in an afternoon, and even be bold enough to call it programmatic SEO. For many brands, it worked, bringing in massive search traffic and organic revenue.

Management teams also buy in easily, because time to market is short and production costs are low.

Those same two things are now what make it fail. Aggressive programmatic SEO initiatives like these are collapsing or drawing manual penalties, because no one asks whether these pages deserve to exist.

Google has been clear about this. On March 5, 2024, it strengthened its scaled content abuse policy to apply whether automation, humans, or a combination produces the pages, and later reported 45% less low-quality, unoriginal content in results.

On Sept. 7, 2026, John Mueller replied on Bluesky to a site that generated pages from every combination of domain names, technologies, and attributes. He wrote that programmatic SEO of that kind often leads to a site that’s spam, borderline spam, or low quality, and that pages already published may keep shaping how Google judges the whole site.

I have been building programmatic SEO systems since 2016, from static templates to natural language generation engines such as Rosae NLG to AI-assisted pipelines. Some compounded for years and became true case studies for me. Some failed fairly quickly. I have taken that work to conference stages along the way, most recently in a session on scaling pSEO at the Shenzhen SEO Conference.

What we see today is mass AI publishing disguised as programmatic SEO. The real thing starts with a dataset that gives every page something a visitor can use. This article draws the line between the two.

Programmatic SEO is a way of publishing, not a kind of content. It has three parts: a repeatable search pattern, a structured dataset that makes each page unique and value-driven, and a template that answers the query for every variation.

Take a currency converter. The pattern is “convert X to Y,” the dataset is a live rate for every currency pair, and the template turns each row into a page. Nobody writes thousands of pages by hand. The data makes each page different. And you publish only as many pages as your data can support.

Lucia Lecesne, the Marketing Lead of Wise, which runs exactly that kind of program, says:

“At Wise, we focus on genuine customer utility: solving a problem that users face on their journey to become customers. Programmatic SEO can then make that solution relevant and accessible across the many search queries and modifiers that share the same problem, in other words, tailoring it to each customer’s specific search context. It should never be a shortcut to publishing large volumes of low-quality pages.”

Mass AI publishing looks the same from the outside, which is why the two get confused. It keeps the template and the publishing system, but what makes each page different comes from a prompt. Swap the city name, and you have a new page with nothing new on it.

Google’s policies draw the same line. The word “programmatic” does not appear in its spam policies. What does appear is scaled content abuse: many pages generated mainly to manipulate rankings rather than help users, no matter how it’s created. Using generative AI to generate many pages without adding value is one of its named examples.

A template isn’t what gets penalized, and neither is automation. The core question worth evaluating is whether each page adds value.

Here is a quick test. Picture two pages for “cost of living in Lisbon,” built from the same template and the same search pattern. The first shows rent ranges, transport passes, and grocery prices pulled from a maintained dataset, and it updates when the numbers change.

The second looks just as complete, with a rent figure, a monthly budget, and a confident summary, but the numbers are the model’s best guess. They carry no source and no date, and the same sentences appear on every other city page with only the name changed. Only the first is programmatic SEO. To tell them apart, ask where each number on the page came from and when it was last updated. The first page can answer. The second can’t.

See also: How Do You Fix Thin Content Across Similar Ecommerce Product Pages? – Ask An SEO

Most teams can’t say whether their pages are programmatic SEO or mass publishing, because the output looks the same from the outside. These six checks look underneath it.

None of these checks ask whether AI wrote the page. A page built on real data and drafted with AI can still perform well, while a hand-written page with no real data behind it has no more claim to rank. Treat the comparison rubric as a diagnostic: if one of the rows fails, you have a workflow problem to fix. If several parameters fail, then you are mass publishing, whatever you call it.

Eli Schwartz draws the line in the same place, and argues:

“Spinning up pages just because you can isn’t SEO; it’s programmatic spam. If you create pages because they benefit many users, that is good SEO, whether you create them programmatically or manually.”

Danny Sullivan, then Google’s Search Liaison, shared a way to test this at a 2025 event. The question, in his words as Search Engine Journal reported, is whether the intent was “‘I’m going to get that traffic’ and not ‘some user actually expected it'” if they came to your site directly. Ask that of your own pages: would a visitor who arrived straight at your site ever land on this one on purpose?

The pages I built in 2016 and the ones I build today look very similar. Shipping a bad one is the part that got easy. I walked through that early scaling playbook at BrightonSEO in 2022.

The middle era is the one I think about most. A rule-based engine like Rosae NLG writes sentences from structured data, and it only says what the data and the template author allow. It was slow to build, and that slowness was doing useful work.

Language models took that limit away. A model will write a fluent, confident paragraph about a row with nothing in it, and a reader cannot tell. I covered where AI belongs in a pSEO pipeline, and where it does not, at ISS Barcelona in 2024.

So the checks evolved. People do the research and decide each page’s structure, the model drafts the sections from that structure, and a subject matter expert reviews the facts and brand fit before anything goes live.

Language models did not make programmatic SEO better or worse. We used to be stopped by the tools. Now we have to stop ourselves, and the checklist below is how I do it.

In my experience, the programs that have survived and thrived across multiple Google updates had a written rule for deleting pages before they needed one.

That is close to how Kevin Indig describes the failure mode in a direct message with me:

“Programmatic SEO usually goes wrong when it is ‘spray and pray: publishing a lot of pages at once with no experimentation, no refreshing, and no look at engagement.’ The fix is the one worth underlining: treat pSEO like its own product, not like a content batch.”

Search is changing underneath these programs. In the first four months of 2026, 68% of U.S. Google searches ended without a click, according to SparkToro’s analysis of Similarweb data. That’s up from about 60% in 2024 and about 45% in 2016. SparkToro points to AI Overviews, which it says now appear on more than 20% of searches, and Ahrefs estimates they cut clicks on the top result by 58%.

For a programmatic page, that changes the goal. Traffic can’t be the only test of whether a page earns its place, because the click may never come. What stays is influence: Rand Fishkin notes that your content still shapes AI answers and Google’s other zero-click features even as visits fall.

“pSEO doesn’t fail because it’s programmatic; it fails when scale replaces substance. The hard part isn’t the tech; it’s the discipline to never trade quality for volume, because pSEO makes that trade tempting for every decision maker.

The test hasn’t changed. If a page’s only value was that it ranked, zero-click search takes away its reason to exist. If the value was the data, an AI answer still has to point to it. Before you scale anything, pick one page and ask where each number on it came from.

#7436. Google Releases Modern Web Guidance 1.0 For AI Coding Agents via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

This webinar uses Conductor's research to help you prioritize marketing data and AI visibility measurement fixes.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: 9 AI Workflows For Better Content. Nov 18, 2 PM ET.

A free skill set for AI coding agents leaves preview with a codebase audit and public evals. One early test scored higher when agents were told to use it.

Google issued version 1.0 of Modern Web Guidance, which is a free skill set that web development teams may use as an enhancement to their AI coding tools, in order for those tools to write code based on current browser features. The skills are in the form of packaged guidelines that the agent will look at while writing the code. The code generated by the agent will also be sent to the same pages that are evaluated for metrics such as Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), Interaction to Next Paint (INP), and accessibility.

Philip Walton, a senior staff developer relations engineer at Google, announced the release in a Chrome for Developers post. Version 1.0 adds an audit for existing code, and Firefox and Edge are joining the project. Chrome first released the guidance as an early preview at Google I/O in May.

Teams can install it by running npx modern-web-guidance@latest install in a project directory. It’s also available through the plugin marketplaces of most popular coding agents, according to the post.

Version 1.0’s audit will go through a project’s HTML, CSS, JavaScript files as well as its package.json to identify areas where developers are able to safely update their code, then walk the agent through the changes. This first iteration of the audit uses static analysis to look at a limited number of code patterns, according to the post.

The post says the library now targets “hundreds of verified AI knowledge gaps” across its guides. Additionally, current coding models continue to fall short in Google’s tests of accessibility, security headers, and loading priority for scripts and images.

According to Google, each of the guides is now reviewed and approved by a domain tech lead. For user-facing feature guides there is a dedicated accessibility review done by experts who use assistive technologies daily.

A governance document was uploaded to the project’s GitHub repository on Nov. 9 which outlines six owner seats for the project. Two of those seats belong to Chrome, Microsoft Edge and Mozilla each have one, and two are given to independent web platform experts. There is currently one open independent seat and no seat belongs to Apple.

Google’s announcement links to a public eval dashboard where coding agents from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google run the same set of tasks every night, with and without the guidance. A real browser then checks the DOM, styles and source code of each finished app.

When I checked Tuesday morning, guided runs were passing 88% of the automated checks, whereas unguided runs were passing 56%. These figures are based upon each agent’s combined results for nightly runs completed Nov. 8; the range is 199 to 215 tasks per agent. The dashboard provides a limited review (not a full WCAG audit, it says) of accessibility features such as support for keyboards, focus, and form labels.

Its task prompts don’t mention the guidance, so each agent has to work out on its own when a guide applies. In most of the recent suites listed, guided runs ran slower and burned more tokens.

Accessibility consultant Adrian Roselli evaluated the preview in May by giving Antigravity (Google’s AI coding tool) an animated accordion prompt found in the documentation. However, according to Roselli, the output did not comply with WCAG and its animation was not functional in Firefox. He also found no assurance that agents would be able to follow the guidelines. This was for the preview, not v1.0.

The new guidelines were tested by Japan’s creator platform, note inc. using two coding agents that ran through six user interface (UI) tasks across 180 test runs on clone versions of note inc.’s production code base. As explained in a Chrome blog, both agents’ scores on 19 browser checks rose after installing the skill without naming it in prompts, then again once prompts named it. Agent One went from 60.8% to 76.5% to 94.0%. Similarly, Agent Two had scores of 75.8%, 86.2%, and 90.0% under the same three test conditions.

One of note’s tasks checked whether the largest image in view on an article page had high priority and wasn’t lazy-loaded. The comparison table in the post shows that unguided agents wrote hero image code using both high priority and lazy loading.

The guidance is run by MetaMask, as part of an automatic review process for each pull request submitted to its open-source browser extension, according to a second Chrome post. Through Oct. 21 (the first five weeks), the bot identified 102 issues across 57 feature and fix pull requests. The engineers fully resolved 43 of them and partially resolved three of them. Another 16 were either declined or false positives. Twenty of them went unaddressed. The outcome of the other 20 is unknown.

Modern Web Guidance provides a no-cost means for teams to encourage agents writing code to use native browser capabilities and that includes code in existing legacy code bases. Most of the results that have been published are based on testing conducted by Google as well as customer testing that Google highlighted. Note Inc. tested the two agents using the same prompt with and without telling them to use the guidance; they both performed better when the prompt did tell them to use the guidance. The team can also label their prompts to include the guidance and keep field data and manual accessibility testing in the review.

Google says it plans to expand this process of auditing existing code at some point, as well as performing audits in which the agent is reasoning about the actual code being audited.

The company suggests pairing the guidance with Chrome DevTools for agents to allow the agent to run its own created code and test it inside of the browser. Preview users can use the command npx modern-web-guidance@latest update.

#7432. Meta expands age detection measures for teens

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The company said it’s implementing more tools to help protect young users, and called on competitors to follow suit.

Meta announced on Monday that it’s expanding its use of its artificial intelligence-powered age estimation technology to ensure that more teens are placed into age-appropriate experiences. The move comes amid ongoing global discussions about teen social media restrictions.

Over the past year, Meta has been working to improve its age detection system, which utilizes visual and contextual analysis to determine a user’s age.

As explained by Meta: “We use AI technology to find people we suspect to be teens, even if they use an adult birthday, and place them in Teen Account protections. Since first introducing this technology, we’ve been placing more teens in age-appropriate protections and are encouraged by the results.”

Meta said that this process has ensured that millions of teens across the world are placed into protective experiences, even when teens misrepresent their age.

“We’re continuing to roll this technology out on Facebook and, later this year, we’ll begin launching similar technology globally on Threads,” Meta said. “This expansion builds on our commitments under our recent agreement with 52 bipartisan attorneys general to strengthen how we identify teens and children under 13 on our apps.”

In August, Meta agreed to pay $18 billion and implement a range of new teen protection measures to settle a landmark lawsuit brought by a coalition of U.S. attorneys general. By settling the case, Meta avoided a trial, which could have put a spotlight on the harms caused by social media.

Some of the measures Meta agreed to implement as part of this settlement included time limits on teen social media usage, blocks on notifications during school times and overnight and the capacity for teen users to set a non-algorithmic feed as the default.

Meta has implemented these measures yet, but as more regions consider similar restrictions, the company appears to want to get out in front of any demands, in order to present itself as taking proactive action.

But Meta would probably not be taking these steps if not for the U.S. attorneys general’s case.

The bigger question, however, is just how effective the company’s automated account estimation and teen detection tools will be. While Meta is keen to highlight the potential here, evidence suggests that this new push won’t be as effective as the company is claiming.

In Australia, for example, Meta said it removed more than 750,000 profiles it detected as belonging to teen users. That move was part of the company’s compliance with Australia’s social media ban for users under age 16, which went into effect in December 2025.

That’s a significant amount. However, a report from Australia’s eSafety Commission published in August indicated that 81.5% of underage users continued to access restricted apps.

That suggests that either Meta’s detection systems are not as effective as the company claims, or teens are simply finding new ways to evade detection.

On Monday, Meta also announced an Australia-specific measure that will see the company incorporateApple’s age-range signal as another means to determine user age.

“The process is simple,” Meta said. “When a parent sets up a smartphone for their teen, they have the option for the app store to confirm the age of the person using the device and assign them an age range. Then, each time the teen downloads an app, Apple passes that age range to the developer — Meta, for example — confirming whether the teen meets the app’s age requirement.”

Meta said it’s voluntarily using this information, while also reiterating its call for app stores to play a bigger role in determining user age at the download level.

Finally, Meta used Monday’s announcement as an opportunity to deflect some of the pressure it’s been under regarding age checking by calling on other platforms to implement similar protections.

“We’ll continue to do our part to proactively ensure teens are in age-appropriate experiences on our apps,” Meta said. “That’s why as part of our agreement with 52 bipartisan attorneys general across US states, territories, and the District of Columbia, we’re investing in even stronger technology to proactively catch accounts that may belong to children under 13. We’re also strengthening the technology we use to identify accounts that may belong to teens between the ages of 13 and 17 so we can ensure those accounts are placed in experiences designed for teens, even if they give us an adult birthday. As Instagram is just one of the many apps teens use, we’re also calling on our industry peers, TikTok and YouTube, to adopt these same practices to keep teens safe.”

It seems like a questionable approach, using the critically important issue of protecting teen users as corporate leverage.

But that's the angle that Meta's going with, as it seeks to dilute the potential impact of such changes on its business.

#7430. “F*** Keywords” – Well, What Are You Replacing Them With? via @sejournal, @chrisgreenseo

This webinar uses Conductor's research to help you prioritize marketing data and AI visibility measurement fixes.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Declaring keywords dead is easy. Explaining what you’ll track, how you’ll govern content, and what stakeholders buy into is the harder part.

Every so often, someone in SEO announces “f*** keywords” or a similar sentiment. It’s not really a “hot take.” Moreover, it’s something that we see time and again.

Sometimes it’s a fair reaction to how reluctant some people in the industry are to change. Other times it feels more like a meme response, or a flex. A way to show you’ve moved on from old-school SEO without saying much about what you do differently, exaggerating a tension between pro/anti keywords without understanding it.

I have some sympathy for the sentiment for sure. I’ve worked on too many campaigns where success came down to whether a handful of keywords went up or down. Once those rankings became THE GOAL, it was easy to spend more time explaining two dropped places than asking whether we met the primary business need. More damagingly, in the worst cases we were left making decisions just for promoting keywords, rather than the business goals they were supposed to enable.

I don’t know how many people still run campaigns that way, and I suspect fewer than the “f*** keywords” cry implies. What interests me is how quickly the argument goes from “this is a bad way to judge a campaign” to “why are we thinking about keywords at all?”

Take an example search like [hotels near Heathrow with a shuttle]. It’s a decent shorthand for what someone wants to know before they book. Is there a shuttle to the terminal? Does it run when my flight lands? Do I need to reserve a seat? It also gives you a clue about what language you need to use to gain recognition from the searcher.

If guests are looking for a shuttle, the page titled “ground transportation solutions” is making them do more work than they need to. Again, a fictitious example, but I have lost track of how many times in my career I’ve seen businesses wanting to target the ways they define their products/services, NOT how people search for them.

In this instance, what is more important is that the initial search query becomes emblematic of a series of questions that need answering, potentially across a series of pages. Whether we call this a hub and spoke model, or a content cluster, whatever, we have captured part of the customer journey with a query and then determined the potential related queries.

This is where a keyword map (or site map) earns its keep, long after the initial research is done and the content written and published. Imagine that six months later someone rewrites a particular location page. The shuttle timetable moves into a general FAQ and a new transfers page goes live. All three changes are totally logical, but taken together, they can leave the site without a clear place to answer the question the location page used to own. Without realizing it, you have sleepwalked into undoing the research you have done before.

If you’ve recorded which page serves that need, the next content editor or SEO has something to go back to. They can ensure that intent/search query is still considered, move content responsibility, update the internal links, and ensure the redirects are done. The keyword map preserves the reasoning behind those original decisions and helps you tell the difference between an intentional change and targeting that drifted over a few rounds of perfectly reasonable edits.

The keywords aren’t the single truth, nor are they to be treated as an immutable dogma, but throwing them in the “f***it bucket” could be missing something important.

Too cool for keywords now? Great, but how does governance work? How do you ensure you’re not wasting the money already spent on research? Yeah, I know – that sounds tedious, because it can be. And building a process to make sure this isn’t painfully manual IS hard.

You can organize your work around topics, and you can use embeddings to help group the language – in fact you should! But at some point, you’ll at least need to benchmark overall visibility, and you still have to choose what to type into a search box or put in a prompt. You can aggregate your rank/prompt tracking for a content cluster – which is needed – but before the aggregation comes selections of individual prompts and terms.

Stakeholders need to buy into those prompts/terms/queries that make up that group OR you 10x the number of specific tracked elements to totally de-emphasize any individual one. Not a bad idea, but you increase your costs significantly and still need to consider the wording, terms and intents on individual pages when it comes to making optimizations.

Instead, I’d happily track a few representative searches for a given page, where I would also want to see which URL(s) appeared and whether they answered the question. Those observations can tell us whether the page is doing some of the work we intended, whether another page is potentially conflicting and where our own content is falling behind competitors.

“Wait, we still use keywords in our data, but we don’t report on the success of individual keywords anymore!” That is perfectly sensible, but it turns out that maybe, perhaps, the “f*** keywords” position is more clickbait than actual smart thinking – right?

These are SEO basics; I totally understand. Prompt tracking and AI search do ultimately de-emphasize the importance of exact keywords in favor of meaning. But consider that embedding text into vectors is so “machines” can understand it. Your team, colleagues and stakeholders still need the human version to understand how to optimize and tell the story of what is/isn’t working.

All of this helps us understand what we’re visible for, but it doesn’t tell us what happened next – and that is perhaps the biggest weakness.

In Search City, I wrote about the temptation to only optimize for the bits of the search journey we can see. Rankings were always one of the easier bits to observe – that is why we have had an almighty job replacing them with a more useful metric, and why the issues hitting prompt trackers are so disruptive to the industry! But now, even when someone makes a search and sees you for that query/keyword/prompt, the part that links that moment to a click and then an important business event can be almost totally disconnected.

Knowing whether we “rank” for a keyword or not is still an important data point. Fixating on that single data point is mad – but that goes for any single data point. We need to use it to build the picture, build a story and provide insight.

If I went back to any of those campaigns I ran where I felt single terms were prioritized (to a fault), I’d probably still keep some of the same keywords – as triggering as that may be.

I’d use them to agree which searches mattered the most, decide which pages should serve them and check whether those pages still do the job. When it came time to judge the campaign, I’d want to know what happened to the customers/clicks we were trying to win. That was the question the rankings were supposed to help us answer in the first place, and it is still something they can help answer today.

This post was originally published on Chris Green SEO.

#7426. Instagram launches visual effects creator for Edits

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The new tool allows users to describe and build effects without the need for coding, and all approved effects will be available for public use in Instagram Stories.

Instagram has launched a web-based, artificial intelligence-powered effects builder option as part of its Edits platform, which will enable users to create and share digital effects for use in Instagram Stories.

The new element of Edits, called Effect Builder, works on conversational prompts, with users able to describe the visual effect they want. The tool will then be able to build it, no coding skills required.

As explained by Instagram product designer Cheechee Lin: “We've seen how much people love Restyle effects in Stories and how quickly a great effect takes off when it's easy to try. But until now, building effects required special design and technical skills. Now with Effect Builder, you don't need design or coding skills, or prior experience making effects. Describe the look you want, preview it on your own photos, and publish.”

As shown in this example screen, the Effect Builder process will provide a range of editable fields and elements, which users can change and refine as they go about building their effect.

Meta also said that images can be used as a style reference “to guide the look of your effect.”

“On the homepage’s prompt box, click Style reference to upload a photo,” Meta said. “Meta AI uses aspects of the image like its color, lighting and texture, to guide the look of your effect.”

Users can also test their effects in the editor to help customize and improve the output.

Once submitted, creator effects will be reviewed by Meta for safety before being made available for anyone else to use on Instagram.

Creators can check in on the status of their in-review effects in the Library tab in Effects Builder, and Meta’s review process will generally take less than 24 hours.

Once an effect is published, it will be available in the Stories effects browser alongside all other Stories effects. Lin said that user-created effects will include a link back to the effect creator’s profile.

The process is essentially an effects extension of the AI Restyle option that Instagram launched in October 2025, which also enabled users to generate visual effects via conversational prompts.

Effects created through that process could also be shared with others, so functionally, this new Effect Builder process is not new. But it does now seem to incorporate more creative elements. Meanwhile, the capacity to build effects via desktop could also lead to more complex, interesting creations.

Edits launched for MacOS last week. It’s the first step in the app’s expansion to desktop and this web-based Effects Builder is another part of that.

Maybe that will lead to more interesting uses of Meta’s AI tools for visual effects in Stories.

Google is expanding ads in AI Mode to 10+ countries in English and launching multiturn ads in the U.S. Here is what PPC advertisers need to know about reporting.

Google is expanding ads in AI Mode to more than 10 new countries in English while launching multiturn ads for follow-up queries in the U.S.

Google shared the update from its official Google Ads X account on November 9, following an earlier LinkedIn post from Dan Taylor noting plans to bring ads in AI Mode to additional countries in Q4.

Eligible campaigns can already participate, though advertisers still can’t see AI Mode performance separately in Google Ads.

Here’s what’s changing, how conversational placements work, and what you need to know when clients ask about AI Mode reporting.

Google’s October announcement named 10 additional countries where ads in AI Mode are expanding:

The expansion currently supports English. Google also announced plans to bring ads in AI Mode to Brazil, Mexico, and the United Kingdom in Q4 2026. Those markets were listed as upcoming rather than part of the initial rollout.

Google’s availability documentation notes that Pakistan supports text ads only.

Multiturn ads are launching in the U.S., allowing ads to appear on follow-up questions within an AI Mode conversation. Google hasn’t announced when those placements will expand outside the U.S.

Google describes AI Mode as a search experience for questions involving exploration, reasoning, or complex comparisons. Users can ask a detailed question an dcontinue with follow-ups as they work through their options.

AI Mode may use “query fan-out,” issuing related searches across subtopics and data sources to develop a response.

With multiturn ads, Google can show an ad during those follow-up exchanges when the conversation has commercial relevance.

According to Google’s advertiser documentation, ads can match directly to a search query or draw on context from both the question and AI response. An exploratory question can then create an advertising opportunity even when the user hasn’t searched for a specific product.

In his LinkedIn update, Taylor noted that people are asking longer, more detailed, and exploratory questions in AI Mode, and described many of those interactions as upper-funnel queries that carry commercial intent.

For advertisers, that means ads may reach people still comparing approaches or deciding what they need. A longer question or another follow-up does not, on its own, indicate that someone is ready to buy.

As ads in AI Mode expand, clients will likely ask whether their campaigns are appearing there and how those ads perform.

In my view, the most important thing for agency and in-house teams to communicate right now is that reporting is limited, and you can’t separate out AI Mode performance granularly.

Google’s reporting documentation confirms that AI Mode impressions, clicks, conversions, and costs are included in standard campaign reporting. Search terms are also combined with other traffic, without a separate AI Mode breakdown. That prevents advertisers from calculating an AI Mode-specific CPA or ROAS.

Google’s keyword prioritization documentation also says reported search terms for experiences including AI Mode may approximate the user’s intent. Advertisers should not assume they are seeing the exact question someone entered.

Teams can still review those terms for relevance, compare conversion performance, and check lead quality. If results change after the rollout, though, the timing alone can’t directly establish that AI Mode caused it.

When clients ask how AI Mode ads are performing, advertisers can explain that those results are included in campaign totals. Google Ads doesn’t report them separately, so teams can’t show how much spend or how many conversions came from AI Mode.

Google is adding countries and follow-up placements without giving advertisers a separate view of their results.

That leaves teams answering questions about AI Mode with campaign-level data. A campaign could improve overall while AI Mode underperforms, or the reverse, and the combined totals wouldn’t show that granularity.

Separate reporting would help advertisers understand which searches and placements are producing sales or qualified leads. Until Google provides it, teams can explain how their campaigns qualify for AI Mode, but can’t necessarily tell clients what those placements contributed to.

Know Python packaging for libraries: pyproject.toml, wheels, modern tooling, version support policy, and why libraries shouldn't pin their dependencies tightly.

Test as a habit: unit, type-level and end-to-end against a real stack. Every fix comes with a regression test.

Write well. Design docs, changelogs and issue replies are a large part of the output here, much of it public, and we're async by default.

#7421. LinkedIn explains its improved content recommendation system

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The company’s Profile Relevance model uses LLM-generated embeddings to show users more relevant posts from people they don’t follow.

LinkedIn shared insights into its evolving content recommendation system, with an overview of its improved, artificial intelligence-powered process. The platform’s system determines what content from non-connections gets displayed to users in their feed.

In a post on the LinkedIn Engineering Blog, LinkedIn engineer Shiyong Lin explained the platform’s new Profile Relevance model, which uses LLM-generated embeddings to match members and posts, based on professional context.

The process essentially summarizes each user’s profile into a prompt, taking into account each member’s profile information and posting history. It then builds a personalized guide of what they’re likely to be interested in.

On a basic level, this means that the system creates a chatbot-style summary of each user’s information, which then dictates what they get shown in the app.

Using these generated summaries, LinkedIn built a new recommendation system that measures content relevance versus each member’s summary.

As per Lin: “The system evaluates how well each post matches a member’s professional context across specific factors, including topic, location, job title, company, industry, seniority, and education.”

LinkedIn assessed these results manually before building a system that showed users more relevant posts from members they don’t follow in the app.

This has led to notable improvements in feed relevance.

As per Lin: “Online experiments recorded a +0.54% lift in Feed Updates Viewed, a +0.94% increase in viral rate, and a -18.8% reduction in hide rate, indicating a more relevant and less noisy member experience. For members, this translates into a feed that surfaces high-quality content beyond their immediate network while remaining aligned with their professional context, even when they have limited historical activity.”

Lin said that this system will also benefit creators by ensuring that their posts will reach relevant audiences beyond their immediate network.

“Notably, for cold-start members with limited activity history, we observed a +17.7% increase in viral engagement and a +1.8% lift in DAU, underscoring the model’s ability to generalize effectively even with sparse interaction data.”

In summary, the post recommendations from non-connections in the LinkedIn feed are likely now more relevant and more valuable, driving a better LinkedIn experience.

#7415. Google’s November 2026 Core Update Starts Rolling Out via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

This webinar uses Conductor's research to help you prioritize marketing data and AI visibility measurement fixes.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Spend less time on publishing and reports, and more on helpful content. November 18, 2 PM ET.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: 9 AI Workflows For Better Content. Nov 18, 2 PM ET.

Google's latest core update is rolling out worldwide in all languages. The company calls it a regular update, and rankings may move during the rollout.

Google began rolling out the November 2026 core update today, according to the Google Search Status Dashboard. The rollout started at 10:06 a.m. PT. Google says the update applies globally and to all languages and may take up to two weeks to complete.

The company’s Search Central account also announced the update on LinkedIn. It’s the third Search core update this year. Google recommends waiting until the rollout is complete before checking your Search Console data.

Google’s Search Status Dashboard entry reads:

“Released the November 2026 core update, which applies globally and to all languages. The rollout may take up to 2 weeks to complete.”

“This is a regular update designed to better surface relevant, satisfying content for searchers from all types of sites.”

The exact wording in that sentence is what Google used for its March core update.

As of posting time, no specific objectives are mentioned on either the dashboard entry or the LinkedIn post. The Search Central blog doesn’t have a post regarding the update either. Google’s core updates page carries a revision date of Dec. 10, 2025.

The May core update finished rolling out on June 2, more than five months before today’s launch. Three spam updates ran in between.

The November update is the eighth ranking update listed on the Search Status Dashboard so far this year.

Some sites may experience rank changes during the rollout of the November core update. Google’s core updates document advises waiting at least a full week after the completion of a core update, then comparing your Search Console data from that week to a week prior to the start of the rollout. Google’s suggested baseline in advance of the November update is a week prior to Nov. 10.

A full two-week rollout would finish around Nov. 24. The week immediately following Nov. 24 will include U.S. Thanksgiving, Black Friday and Cyber Monday. Retail sites looking at this time period compared to a pre-update week would be looking at holiday traffic against a regular week.

According to Google, core updates don’t target specific sites or individual pages and are meant to keep its systems current as content on the web changes.

Per its LinkedIn post, Google will update its ranking release history page once the rollout is complete. We’ll update this article then, too.

#7413. TikTok updates its AI video ad tools

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The company’s Symphony platform now has access to the latest model from Dreamina Seedance, offering brands expanded creation options.

TikTok has added some new elements to its artificial intelligence-powered Symphony ad creation tools, including advanced video generation using the latest models, an updated Symphony API and broader access to AI usage tokens.

First, TikTok added more capacity to generate video ads using the latest Dreamina Seedance AI models within its Symphony Agent tool.

As shown in this example sequence, TikTok’s Symphony now has access to the updated visual generation capacity of Dreamina Seedance to generate better-looking ads based on expanded prompts, with users able to integrate example videos and ads.

TikTok said advertisers will now be able to upload up to 50 multimodal references (images, videos, and audio), up from 9 previously, while the updated Seedance models will now be able to generate up to 30 seconds of video for each prompt, up from a previous 15-second maximum.

TikTok said the latest Dreamina Seedance model is also able to generate sharper, more realistic imagery and offer better lighting and character consistency across video frames.

The viability of AI-generated video on TikTok will vary, but it could be worth experimenting with these new video generation tools, based on expanded creative inputs, to see what the system can generate.

TikTok also launched an updated Symphony API, which will enable advertisers to generate content using Symphony’s tools within their own creative management tools.

The company also expanded access to its BytePlus tokens, which will enable more use of its Symphony tools for visual generation.

“Starting November 9, advertisers outside North America can purchase BytePlus tokens to access Dreamina Seedance AI models through Symphony, enabling faster video generation, higher-quality output, and more formats,” TikTok said.

BytePlus is the enterprise technology arm of TikTok parent company ByteDance, and it manages all of the company’s AI tools and systems.

These updates could provide additional considerations for advertisers heading into peak shopping season.

Fingerprint's device intelligence platform processes billions of identification events for companies that need to know who — or what — is on the other end of a request. Increasingly, the answer is not a person. AI agents, AI assistants, crawlers, headless browsers, and malicious automation now make up a large and fast-growing share of internet traffic, and telling them apart from humans — and from each other — is becoming one of the most important problems our customers ask us to solve.

We are standing up a dedicated Automation Intelligence engineering team to own that problem end to end: detection in the browser, detection at the edge, the classification taxonomy that tells customers what kind of automation they're seeing and how confident we are, and the API that customers and their agents call.

We're looking for an Engineering Manager to lead this team. You'll inherit a small, senior group (three engineers to start, growing to four or five) and a clear mandate. You report directly to the VP of Engineering.

This is a hands-on-adjacent engineering manager role for a small, senior, high-leverage team. You are not expected to write the production code — your engineers and their agents do that — but you are expected to be close enough to it to set direction, evaluate the work, and hold the quality bar.

The team has unusual autonomy and unusual visibility. It owns a product that leadership considers strategically critical, it is the first team operating Fingerprint's AI-native engineering model, and its results — good and bad — will be used as evidence for how the rest of engineering works. That means two things: you'll have real room to decide how the team operates, and you'll need to be honest about what the data shows.

In the first 90 days you will likely: finalize the roster and ownership lines with the sibling team, get the quality loop and engineering baselines running, deliver the engineering evidence for the Beta gate, and run the first review of the AI-native operating model.

#7409. Reddit tests AI-compiled product reviews

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The new feature is designed to help users get recommendations and information by converting platform comments into overviews.

Reddit is testing a new Reddit Reviews option, which will help users find relevant product recommendations and info in the app by converting relevant Reddit comments into dedicated overviews.

As shown in these example screens, Reddit Reviews will use artificial intelligence to collate information on products, sourcing relevant references from comments and mentions across the app. The tool will then present comments and upvotes in a centralized review format, which should make it easier for users to gather context about a prospective purchase.

As explained by Reddit: “Lived experience shows up across Reddit communities: in r/skincareaddiction, people share what they’ve tried for dry skin, and in r/espresso, baristas and home brewers compare their setups. These exchanges show how a product can work for different people and what tradeoffs they consider. Reddit Reviews uses AI to both organize these conversations where people describe their product experiences, and to surface the nuance, context, and connection to the original conversation.”

Reddit said these reviews may also include images, prices and purchase links when they’re supplied by brand and retailer catalogs.

“To go deeper, people can browse all comments about a product, using topic filters derived from Reddit conversations to focus on their questions,” Reddit said. “Clicking on a comment lets them read the original discussion, ask a follow-up question, or join the community for more advice. For people considering alternatives, the review also highlights products people commonly compare.”

To find a review, Reddit users can search for a product or category in the app. Products with a review page will be highlighted in the predictive answers to the query.

Reddit said it will initially test the option “with a set of frequently discussed products and categories.”

Reddit added that these reviews will only include information gleaned from organic conversations within Reddit communities, and that these recommendations will not include paid placement of any kind.

Reddit is working to find more ways to get people coming directly to its app for insights because its referral traffic from search engines has been rapidly declining.

Amid rising use of AI chatbots for discovery, Reddit had become a critical source of information due to its user-generated, community-voted listings, which allowed chatbots and search engines to offer direct insights into consumer experiences.

But Google has been putting more emphasis on AI overviews, which provide an AI-generated summary of these notes within search results, while ChatGPT has also reduced its reliance on Reddit data. As a result, Reddit has suffered a big loss in terms of search referrals.

In the company’s Q3 performance update published earlier this month, Reddit CEO Steve Huffman said that the company’s search traffic dropped by more than 1 million referrals on average per week in October.

Given this, Reddit is working to build more valuable tools to drive direct traffic. The company is also experimenting with locking down more of its information, making it only available to logged-in users.

Reddit Reviews is another step in this direction as the platform looks for ways to maintain the value of its app.

#7407. TikTok tests shopping subscriptions

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The company invited select users in the U.S. to join its TikTok Shop Plus program, which will cost about $10 a month after a free trial period.

TikTok is trying out another way to get more people shopping in its app with the launch of a new TikTok Shop Plus subscription option that offers discounts and deals for repeat buyers.

As reported by Modern Retail, TikTok began inviting selected U.S. users over the weekend to join its new TikTok Shop Plus program. Additional reporting from GeekSeller suggested that TikTok has been gradually rolling out the option over the last month.

As per Modern Retail: “TikTok Shop Plus costs $9.99 a month after a 30-day free trial, according to TikTok Shop. It includes perks such as expanded free shipping, exclusive discounts, coupon bundles and instant refunds.”

The offering is similar to Amazon Prime and other subscription shopping options, which are designed to increase customer loyalty through add-on benefits.

It’s TikTok’s latest effort to get more people to buy products on the platform as it works to build a bigger revenue stream through in-app shopping.

TikTok owner ByteDance saw significant success with in-stream shopping via Douyin, the version of TikTok available in China. With Douyin, ByteDance was able to successfully transition short-form video engagement into livestream shopping, which has since generated billions of dollars for the company.

According to KrAsia, Douyin generated nearly $500 billion in gross merchandise volume in 2025, with livestream commerce in particular driving a significant portion of that activity.

That’s likely why Douyin has been working to make in-stream shopping a bigger element of the TikTok experience as well. However, TikTok users have so far been less open to shopping in the app.

That may be changing over time, though. According to Marketing Maze, TikTok generated $26.2 billion GMV in the first half of 2025.

That’s still a long way from Douyin’s result, the numbers make it clear why ByteDance is so enamored with the opportunity, and why the company keeps looking for ways to get more people searching for products and making in-stream purchases.

A loyalty program could help on this front by encouraging the most active shoppers to keep buying from TikTok merchants, in the hopes that this will lead to further endorsements and promotions of TikTok’s shopping experience.

Patrick Nommensen, TikTok Shop’s president of strategic initiatives, told Modern Retail that the program is currently being tested “with an expanding group of eligible U.S. users.”

#7404. Meta Paused Its New Business Terms, And Businesses Should Plan As If It Never Gets Better via @sejournal, @slobodanmanic

This webinar uses Conductor's research to help you prioritize marketing data and AI visibility measurement fixes.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Spend less time on publishing and reports, and more on helpful content. November 18, 2 PM ET.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Meta removed ‘train’ from its crawl clause, kept ‘develop’, then paused everything. The pushback worked once. Do not expect it to work twice.

Meta backed down this time. On Nov. 5, it paused new business terms that would have let it crawl the website of every business using Facebook or Instagram, after publishers, a court, and a regulator pushed back. Pushback can work. But a business that gets its customers through Meta should plan as if Meta will never get better for it.

In October 2026, Meta previewed new business terms, the rules a business accepts when it uses Facebook or Instagram for business: a Page, ads, a shop. The first version let Meta use automated software to read the websites tied to a business, to “provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain” its products. Accepting was the price of staying, and the only way to say no was to stop using Meta for business.

On Oct. 16, Meta took the word “train” out and limited the crawl to its advertising and business products. “Develop” stayed in, and so did the crawl. On Oct. 23, Meta moved the start date from Oct. 30 to Nov. 20.

Meta doesn’t say why it paused. Paused is not withdrawn. Nieman Lab reports Meta’s notice says “our existing terms remain in effect”, and nothing in it says what comes back, or when.

Meta has done things that work for Meta since forever, with no regard for anyone. This is what Meta does. Hollywood has made two films about Facebook, and neither is about how well it treats its users.

Meta’s pattern feels like a slow death for a business in the Meta ecosystem, with nothing it can do about what Meta changes. Reaching for a business’s website is new. The attitude isn’t new: Meta not caring about its business users, and trying to give them no options.

So start investing in other acquisition channels, or at least planning for them.

Meta backed down this time. Do not wait for it to do it again.

This post was originally published on No Hacks.

Featured Image: Jack_the_sparow/Shutterstock

No. On Nov. 5, 2026, Meta paused them. Its Business Help Center says the updates to its Commercial Terms, Product Catalog Terms, Self-Serve Ad Terms, and Ad Creative Generative AI Terms will not take effect on Nov. 20, 2026, and Nieman Lab reports the notice says the existing terms remain in effect. Meta has not said what comes back, or when.

Under the terms Meta previewed in October 2026, a business using Facebook or Instagram for business would have agreed to let Meta’s automated software read its website for Meta’s ads and business products, with no opt-out short of leaving. Those terms are paused. A Meta spokesperson told Nieman Lab that robots.txt preferences are respected.

Yes. On Oct. 30, 2026 the U.K.’s Competition and Markets Authority opened a formal investigation into whether Meta’s commercial terms for businesses using its platforms breach competition law, under the Competition Act 1998. The CMA set no deadline and has made no decision.
